new_entities.name: Urinary tract infection recurrence in women

edges.effect_quant: The strongest recent syntheses suggest cranberry products modestly reduce recurrence risk in women prone to UTIs, although individual trials have not all pointed the same way. The signal is real enough to support a cautious protective classification, but not strong enough to displace better-supported options like vaginal estrogen in postmenopausal recurrence.
edges.population: adult women with a history of recurrent urinary tract infection
edges.mechanism: Cranberry proanthocyanidins can reduce adherence of uropathogenic E coli to the urothelium, making recolonization and recurrence less likely. That anti-adhesion model fits why benefit, when present, is preventive rather than curative.
edges.summary: Cranberry extract appears to modestly reduce recurrent UTI risk in women, but the effect is uneven across trials. Modern meta-analyses lean protective overall, even though some well-known individual randomized trials were neutral.
edges.caveats: Benefit depends on formulation, dose standardization, and adherence, and cranberry juice studies do not always generalize to concentrated extracts or capsules. This edge is best read as low-risk, modest prevention rather than high-certainty prophylaxis.

evidence.notes: Cranberry Reduces the Risk of Urinary Tract Infection Recurrence in Otherwise Healthy Women: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.

effect_quant.comparator: cranberry intervention versus placebo or control in women at risk of recurrent UTI

evidence.citation: Williams et al 2023 Cochrane Database Syst Rev
evidence.notes: Cranberries for preventing urinary tract infections.
